title: The desperado: sell a doomed piece dearly
outcomes: Spots a piece that is lost anyway and has a capture available
Finds the capture that gets the most for it
Counts what the capture wins and what the recapture costs
Says when nothing can be sold: the piece can be saved, or it has nothing to take

steps.text: A **desperado** is a piece that will be lost whatever you do. Before it goes, let it capture as much as it can. When one of your pieces is attacked and every square it can reach is attacked too, ask what it can take on the way out. It cannot be saved, so each capture cuts the loss.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on b7 attacks the knight, and Black attacks every square the knight can reach.

line.say: Nxb8: the doomed knight takes the rook before it falls.
The king recaptures. White gave a knight and won a rook.

claims.statement: Nxb8 is the engine's first choice.
The knight on a6 is attacked and no white piece defends it.
If White simply passes, Black wins the knight (engine line).
After Nxb8 the piece on b8 can be recaptured.
Nxb8 gains material along the engine line.
Nb4 (a retreat) loses at least 700 centipawns compared with the best move.
Nc5 (a retreat) loses at least 600 centipawns compared with the best move.
Nc7 (a retreat) loses at least 500 centipawns compared with the best move.
After Nb4 the knight on b4 is attacked (by the pawn on a5) and no white piece defends it.
After Nc5 the knight on c5 is attacked (by the pawn on d6) and no white piece defends it.
After Nc7 the knight on c7 is attacked (by the king) and no white piece defends it.

steps.text:
Two checks before you sell a piece.
**Is it really lost?** If it has a safe square, saving it may be better. A defender does not help against a pawn.
**What does each capture allow?** Count the recaptures, and compare with losing the piece for nothing.
*Rule of thumb:* counting values (1, 3, 3, 5, 9) are only a guide. A capture that opens a mating line can matter more.
